Green Routing · Per-link forecasting for carbon accounting

Can one model forecast every link well enough to bill its carbon?

A single global forecaster across a national research backbone, tested at year scale on the horizons the carbon bill needs — 8 hours and 1 day ahead. This is the walk-through: the problem, the method, what works, what fails, and what it would take to ship.

01

Start from the bill, not the model

We want a fair, per-user carbon bill for the traffic each user pushes across the network — and to route around dirty power before the load arrives. Both need one thing: a per-link forecast of volume.

Every 5 min, on every link, measure E= CO₂ (kg/min)and V= volume (/min).
A user sendingT GB on that link this window owes   EV×T  — emission per byte, times bytes sent.

The bill is settled from measured E and V. But to schedule, cap and green-route you must know the volume before it happens — so the whole system reduces to one modelling problem: forecast V per link, 8 h and 1 day ahead.

→ Before any results, one question has to be answered plainly: what is a forecast here, and how is it produced?

02

How a forecast is made — one model, a sliding window

Every number in this talk comes from the same five-step loop, run independently on each link. There is one global network shared across all 534 links — not one model per link.

  1. 1Take a windowAt the current 5-min step, read that link's last 1 week (2,016 steps).
  2. 2Normalizelog1p (traffic is log-normal) + RevIN (subtract the window's own mean/std), so a 64 Gbps core port and a 1 Mbps access port share one model.
  3. 3Emit the pathOne forward pass outputs the whole future path at 5-min resolution — direct, not step-by-step, so errors don't compound.
  4. 4Read 1 h / 8 h / 1 dayThey're the first 12 / 96 / 288 steps of that same path; invert the transforms → Mbps.
  5. 5Re-forecastSlide forward and repeat — a fresh forecast every 5 minutes. §06 shows this running.

→ "One model for every link" is a strong claim. So the real work was testing it honestly — where most forecasting projects quietly go wrong.

03

The honest test

Of 1,923 raw interface series on 208 devices, 886 links are usable and 534 carry real traffic (mean ≥ 1 Mbps). Three rules keep the evaluation trustworthy.

Strictly chronological

Train on the past, validate on a later block, test on a still-later 111-day window that crosses the semester → summer boundary and holds 6 Swiss holidays. Scalers fit on train only — no leakage.

Rolling origin

The forecaster is re-run at 160 origins across the test window; at each, it sees only the past. This is walk-forward evaluation, not a single lucky split.

The honest metric

Headline = per-link median error ratio vs. persistence (+ sign tests) — a vote every link casts equally. Pooled Mbps MAE is a traffic-weighted vote the giant links own, so we never lead with it.

→ With the test fixed, we climbed a ladder of models — keeping each one only if it clearly beat the simpler tier below it.

04

The model ladder — why each is here

Complexity is a cost; every tier has to earn it. Verdicts are at the carbon-bill horizons (year-scale, 8 h & 1 day).

Tier 1Baselines
Persistence, seasonal-naive, historical average. Traffic = strong short-term autocorrelation + a daily/weekly cycle — most of the signal with zero learning.
the bar Everything above is scored as skill over these. Persistence is brutal at 1 step; the seasonal naives never win at 8 h / 1 day.
Tier 3GBDT
Forecasting as tabular regression: lag + rolling + calendar features, one global boosted-tree model, a direct regressor per horizon.
wins 1 week · ties 8 h/1 day A full year of seasonal data revives the tree. The cheap, strong workhorse.
Tier 4GRU
A gated recurrent state learns nonlinear temporal dynamics end-to-end instead of hand-built lags.
wins 1 hour Best per-link median and pooled at 1 h; a dependable all-rounder across the board.
Tier 4TCN
Dilated causal convolutions: an exponentially growing receptive field, trained fully in parallel — long memory without recurrence.
wins 1 day Best per-link median & pooled at 1 day, best at 15 min, and the biggest beneficiary of calendar features (§07).
Tier 5DLinear
A single linear layer on a trend/seasonal split — the "Are Transformers Effective?" control. If a linear map matches your transformer, the transformer isn't earning its cost.
control Strong at short horizons, honest elsewhere, and bit-identical across runs — our determinism anchor.
Tier 5PatchTST
A patch-token transformer: attention over a week of patches, with our custom low-rank head.
contender everywhere Ties for best at 8 h, 2nd at 1 h/1 day. It infers the calendar itself, so calendar features hurt it — and are switched off.
Tier 6STGNN
Graph WaveNet
Diffusion over the link graph + a learned adjacency. Links are physically coupled — a reroute shifts load between them together — a signal a per-link model can't see.
GPU-blocked at year scale At week scale it reached GRU-class accuracy with the best 1-hour peak behaviour, but it won't fit the year-scale run on 6 GB (see §09).

→ Here is how they actually scored — with one result that reframes which horizon matters most.

The 8-hour result — a gift for carbon billing

Skill is not monotonic in horizon. The model beats persistence hardest at 8 h (~45%), because 8 h lands off the daily cycle: persistence predicts "8 h from now = now", but 8 h later is a different time of day — a trough where there was a peak — so its error actually peaks at 8 h (pooled 1541 Mbps, worse than at 1 day's 1061). At 1 h persistence is nearly right, and at 1 day it lands on the same time tomorrow, so the model's relative advantage is smaller there. The 8-hour planning window — a work shift — is exactly where a learned model is worth the most.

→ A leaderboard is a vote. Let's watch the model forecast — the sliding window from §02, made visible.

06

Watch it forecast — one method, three scales

The same six links throughout — a giant backbone port, a clean-diurnal link, a weekend-driven one, a bursty one, a deliberately hard one, and a typical mid-size link. Grey is the actual 5-min traffic; coloured lines are the models' forecast paths. (GBDT is direct-per-horizon, so it has no 5-min path — these show the sequence models.)

Scale 1 — the whole test window (111 days)

Does it hold up over a full season? Yes: the 1-day path tracks the level and weekly rhythm from March to July, straight through the semester→summer drop. No drift blow-up.

Scale 2 — three weeks, three horizons

Zoom in and switch the block length. The rule is clean: the shorter the lead, the tighter the forecast hugs the actual. At 1 day the model draws the whole diurnal arc in advance; the peaks are where it's shaved.

Scale 3 — a single forecast block

All the way in — about one day, and about eight hours. You can watch one path track the actual at 5-min resolution and re-forecast at the seam, snapping back to the latest level.

Captures the shape. Diurnal and weekly rhythm, deep weekend drops, slow level drift — all tracked. The weekend-driven link (0.57× at 1 day) is where calendar features pay off most.
Shaves the peaks. Coloured lines sit below the grey spikes — the operationally dangerous error for capacity planning. We attacked it directly (§07).
Fails on noise. The hard link (sgd2, 1.45× at 1 day) is so bursty the smooth global path misses it — the model loses to persistence there.
…but not everywhere. That same hard link tracks fine at 1 h — its failure is horizon-specific, and it's part of a stable ~11% tail that §08 is built for.

→ The plots expose exactly two gaps — shaved peaks and an unreachable tail. We went after both.

07

What we improved

Four changes this cycle — the first three target gaps you just saw in the plots, the fourth makes every number trustworthy.

Peak-aware training → the shaved peaks

Every learned model under-predicted each link's top-decile peaks by 36–46%. An asymmetric loss (under-predictions cost 2×, in train and validation) lifts the forecast: day-horizon peak bias −40% → −27%, under-prediction rate 0.90 → 0.75 — for mild off-peak over-prediction.

Calendar features → weekends & holidays

Day-of-week + Swiss holidays as known-future covariates. Seed-clean verdict: helps TCN (day −5%, 78% of links), GRU and GBDT; hurts PatchTST (its attention already infers it → off). DLinear stays the untouched control.

PatchTST low-rank head → a broken tier

The paper's flatten head (~65 M params) memorised the train regime by epoch 2; a naïve attention-pooled replacement over-corrected. A flatten → 384-d bottleneck → horizon head (~13 M) took PatchTST from worst learned tier to contender.

Trustworthy numbers → reproducibility

Fixed a shared-RNG bug (per-model seeding, bit-reproducible) and a validation criterion blind to long horizons (a single seed once swung day-MAE 13.5%; now ±3–4%). Measured noise floor ≈ ±1% median — the 8 h column matched the original run bit-for-bit.

→ One gap can't be closed by training harder: the ~11% of links the global model structurally can't fit. That's a modelling-shape problem, not a tuning one.

08

From one global model to per-link

The global model already wins on 89% of links at 1 day. The remaining tail isn't random noise — it's a stable set of idiosyncratic links (like the hard case in §06), and it's exactly what a per-link stage should own.

89% — global beats persistence (median 0.72× at 1 day)
11% tail
Global wins — one cheap shared model, generalises to new links Global loses / ties (8% by >1.1×) — the fine-tuning target

The hybrid

Keep the global net as a shared backbone — it carries the structure common to all links and covers 89% of them. Add a lightweight per-link head / adapter for identity: broad skill and tail robustness, without one model per link from scratch.

Already built

The harness can warm-start from the global net and fine-tune a few low-LR epochs on each link's recent history at test time (leakage-guarded). The mechanism a per-link stage needs already exists — today it's gated by compute, not design.

Why the tail matters for the bill

The bill's error is dominated by the highest-volume links (largest E/V·T) and by the tail links billed wrong. Per-link fine-tuning targets both — tightening the giant backbone ports and rescuing the 1.45× failures — for a fairer, tighter carbon bill.

→ Fine-tuning 534 links, plus the graph model and foundation models, is one thing away: compute.

09

The one lever left — GPU

Every result here was produced on a single laptop RTX 3060 with 6 GB. It was enough to prove the method — and it is now the ceiling on the research. This isn't hypothetical: rendering the §06 paths, a 6-link inference batch ran the GPU out of memory (needed 7.9 GB) and had to be split.

Today · RTX 3060 Laptop · 6 GB

  • The graph model (STGNN) — best 1-hour peak behaviour — won't fit the year-scale run.
  • 6 GB forces tiny batches; even inference is split to avoid OOM.
  • No multi-seed error bars and no per-link fine-tuning at scale — they don't finish.
  • Foundation models (TimesFM / Chronos) are out of reach entirely.

With a datacenter GPU (A100 / H100)

  • Per-link fine-tuning for all 534 links — close the 11% tail, tighten the biggest-volume ports.
  • STGNN & foundation models at year scale — the spatial / reroute signal, finally tested.
  • Multi-seed runs → honest error bars instead of single-seed point estimates.
  • ~10 h → <1 h iteration: bigger models, longer lookback, and the online-adaptation experiments per-link billing needs.

In one line: the benchmark is validated, the 8-hour horizon is where the model pays off most, and the per-link mechanism is built. GPU is the single lever between this prototype and a deployable, per-user carbon-accounting forecaster.
